result.summary: Pausanias continues his tour of Megara and its territory, describing temples, monuments and tombs in the city, at Nisæa, Pagæ, Ægosthena and Erenea. He then follows the Scironian road toward Corinth, recounting the legends of Ino, Sciron, Eurystheus and Hyllus.

scenes.title: Megara city: Orsippus and temples
scenes.summary: Pausanias notes Orsippus's tomb and the Megarian temples of Apollo, Artemis, Leto and Ilithyia.

scenes.title: Nisæa and Minoa
scenes.summary: At the dockyard are the temple of Demeter, the tomb of Lelex and the island of Minoa.

scenes.title: Pagæ, Ægosthena and Erenea
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes sights in the mountain towns, including the tombs and shrines of Ægialeus and Melampus, and Autonoe's tomb.

scenes.title: Tombs and the Scironian road
scenes.summary: Along the road to Corinth are tombs and the shell-stone of Megara; the road was made by Sciron and widened by Adrian.

scenes.title: Molurian rock and Sciron
scenes.summary: Ino leaps into the sea with Melicerta, who becomes Palæmon; Sciron is punished by Theseus.
scenes.stakes: Ino and her son flee the mad Athamas; strangers are thrown into the sea by Sciron.

scenes.title: Mountain top to the border
scenes.summary: Shrines on the mountain, the tomb of Eurystheus and the Corinthian border where Hyllus fought Echemus.

alias_notes.explanation: Melicerta was honoured under the name Palæmon after being carried by a dolphin to the Isthmus.
Ino is worshipped as Leucothea, a sea goddess, though this section names the rock sacred to Leucothea and Palæmon.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias's rationalising explanation of Orsippus's naked running.
Sciron's fate: he suffers the death he inflicted on others.

analysis.text: Pausanias blends sights with local legend, and explains place names and customs through myth, with a poetic justice in Sciron's fate.
Mention of Hadrian's road works shows Roman imperial investment in Greek infrastructure, while Megarian tradition preserves its own local heroes.

legacy.text: The Isthmian games' link to Palæmon and the legend of Sciron's cliffs fed later Greek and Roman literature, including Ovid's Metamorphoses.

fun_facts.text: Megara's shell-bearing white limestone was used in many buildings, as Pausanias notes.

language_notes.text: "Next Corœbus is buried Orsippus" is inverted and elliptical: Orsippus's tomb lies next to that of Corœbus, mentioned just before.
"Cut off a slice" means he annexed part of the neighbouring territory by conquest.
"Protecting Apollo" translates a cult title (Prostaterios) for Apollo as guardian; the epithet marks his protective role.
"Dockyard" here means the harbour town of Megara, Nisæa, on the coast.
The war with Nisus: King Minos of Crete besieged Megara, ruled by Nisus, using Minoa as a naval base.
The Medes here mean the Persians, whose invading army in 479 BC was harassed by Megarian defenders; the arrows were kept as a memorial.
A hero-chapel is a small shrine where a dead hero received cult honours, lower than those paid to gods.
The second march against Thebes is the war of the Epigoni, sons of the Seven; Ægialeus alone of them fell.
Actæon was torn apart by his own hounds, in the best-known version after seeing Artemis bathing; Autonoe was his mother.
This Cleopatra was sister of Alexander the Great; Philip is Philip II of Macedon.
Shell-like stone is a limestone full of embedded seashells, described further in sentence 28.
"Accursed" means under a curse, polluted by Sciron's crimes, so avoided as unlucky.
"The whirligig of time" means the turning wheel of time, which brings retribution; the sentence is slightly broken in grammar, as the translation is literal.
"The Remover" translates a cult title of Zeus, explained in the next sentence as the god who removed the drought.
The Heraclidæ were the descendants of Hercules, who fought Eurystheus, the king who had imposed the labours on Hercules.
"Latoan" means of Leto, Apollo's mother; Latoan Apollo is Apollo as son of Latona.

context_notes.text: Orsippus was a Megarian runner, traditionally said to have won the stadion race at Olympia in 720 BC, the first to run naked.
Praxiteles was a famous Athenian sculptor of the 4th century BC.
Lelex was a legendary early king of Megara, said here to be of Egyptian descent through Libye.
Artemis Saviour was a protective title; Megara also had a statue of her under this name.
Melampus was a legendary seer of Argos, famed for understanding animals and curing madness.
Adrian is the Roman emperor Hadrian (reigned AD 117–138), who sponsored many public works in Greece.
Ino was a daughter of Cadmus and second wife of Athamas; she later became the sea goddess Leucothea.
The Isthmian games were held near Corinth, in honour of Poseidon and, in this tradition, Palæmon.
Eurystheus was the king of Mycenae who set Hercules his labours and persecuted his children.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias shows himself a rationalizing, practical observer, offering his own plausible explanation instead of a legend.
The brisk summary is typical of Pausanias's guidebook manner, closing one stage of the tour before moving on.
A shrine honours a famous prophet, yet locals say he gives no prophecy, an odd contrast Pausanias reports without comment.
Pausanias distinguishes what he heard from what he saw, marking local tradition as hearsay.
Athamas's madness and misjudged blame of Ino show a man driven by rage and false reasoning, mistaking divine famine for human plotting.
Sciron suffers the very fate he inflicted on strangers, a poetic justice that makes his punishment fitting.
